lecture_title: AST 101 Week 1: The Sky Above Us

slides.title: AST 101 Week 1: The Sky Above Us
body_text: Dr. Alex Morgan
Example College
slides.speaker_notes: Start with a sky report: the Moon's phase, when it rises, and one thing to look for tonight.

slides.title: Look Up
body_text: What do you already know about the night sky?
Write down one thing you have noticed about the stars or the Moon
slides.speaker_notes: Collect a few answers. They usually include a misconception or two worth saving for later weeks.

slides.title: The Celestial Sphere
body_text: An imaginary sphere centered on the observer
Stars appear fixed to its inside surface
A model for locating objects, not a physical shell
slides.speaker_notes: Picture an open umbrella over your head with stars painted on the inside. The handle points at the celestial pole.

slides.title: Landmarks on the Sphere
body_text: Zenith: the point straight overhead
Horizon: where the sky meets the ground
North and south celestial poles: Earth's axis extended into the sky
Celestial equator: Earth's equator extended onto the sky
slides.speaker_notes: Have students point to each one with their arms before reading the definitions.

slides.title: The Sky Turns
body_text: Earth rotates west to east once every 24 hours
So the sky appears to rotate east to west, about 15 degrees per hour
Long-exposure photos show star trails as circles around the celestial pole
slides.speaker_notes: Office chair demonstration: spin slowly and the whole room seems to go around you.

slides.title: Polaris and Your Latitude
body_text: Polaris lies within 1 degree of the north celestial pole
The altitude of Polaris above the horizon equals your latitude
At the equator Polaris sits on the horizon; at the North Pole it is overhead
slides.speaker_notes: Polaris is not the brightest star in the sky. It is about the 50th. It is famous for where it is, not how bright it is.

slides.title: Circumpolar Stars
body_text: Stars closer to the pole than your latitude never set
At 45 degrees north, the Big Dipper and Cassiopeia are always above the horizon
Near the equator, almost every star rises and sets
slides.speaker_notes: Ask: from the North Pole, which stars are circumpolar? All of the ones you can see, and none of the southern ones.

slides.title: Hand Angles
body_text: At arm's length, your little finger is about 1 degree wide
Three middle fingers together: about 5 degrees
A closed fist: about 10 degrees
A spread hand, thumb to little finger: about 20 degrees
slides.speaker_notes: The full Moon is only about half a degree across. It hides behind your little finger, which surprises everyone.

slides.title: Smaller Units
body_text: 1 degree = 60 arcminutes
1 arcminute = 60 arcseconds
The full Moon is about 30 arcminutes across
The sharpest human eye resolves about 1 arcminute
slides.speaker_notes: Same pattern as hours, minutes and seconds. Arcseconds come back in AST 102 for star distances.

slides.title: Observing Log, Entry 1
body_text: Find the Big Dipper and follow its two pointer stars to Polaris
Measure the altitude of Polaris in fists
Record the date, time, location and sky conditions
slides.speaker_notes: Cloudy all week? Describe the clouds and the entry still counts. Inventing an observation does not.
